This article is a guide to help you create your own version of the site using Adritian. It will cover the main steps to get started with the theme, and how to customize it to your needs.
Creating a site This theme is for the content management system Hugo, so that will be a pre-requirement. Make sure that you install the extended version of Hugo, as the theme uses SCSS for styling, as well as image optimization.
A very good place to start is the Quick start guide: https://gohugo.io/getting-started/quick-start/
💡Tip:_ keep your repository clean and tidy by creating a relevant .gitignore file since the beginning:
# Generated files by hugo/public//resources/_gen//assets/jsconfig.jsonhugo_stats.json# Executable may be added to repositoryhugo.exehugo.darwinhugo.linux# Temporary lock file while building/.hugo_build.lock Adding the theme Once you have a site created, you can add the theme to your site by following the instructions in the README. While there are multiple ways to add the theme, the recommended way is to use the Hugo Modules, the ones listed here.
Instructions to setup the theme as a hugo moduleCreate a new Hugo site (this will create a new folder): hugo new site <your website's name> Enter the newly created folder: cd <your website's name>/ Initialize the Hugo Module system in your site if you haven’t already: hugo mod init github.com/username/your-site (you don’t need to host your website on GitHub, you can add anything as a name) Replace the contents of your config file (hugo.toml) file by these: hugo.toml configurationbaseURL = "<your website url>"languageCode = "en"[module][module.hugoVersion]# We use hugo.Deps to list = 5listStyle = "summary" # options: simple, summary This configuration allows you to have a base to edit and adapt to your site, and see the available functionalities. Make sure to edit baseURL, title and description. You can edit the header links, as well as the languages to your needs.
Get the module: hugo mod get -u Execute hugo mod npm pack - this will generate a package.json file in the root folder of your site, with the dependencies for the theme. Execute npm install - this will install the dependencies for the theme (including bootstrap) (Optional, to override the defaults) Create a file data/homepage.yml with the contents of the exampleSite/data/homepage.yml file, and customize to your needs. Start Hugo with hugo server… 🎉 The theme is alive on http://localhost:1313/ (if everything went well) Editing the theme content Currently the theme content is spread over multiple folders and files. We are working on simplifying this - but for now this guide should help you get started.
Some of the key files are:
config.toml: Main configuration for your Hugo site. Here you can set the site title, description, and theme specific settings such as:
menu structure (footer and header) analytics (vercel, google) blog settings (layout, sidebar contents, etc) As well as some required settings for the theme to work properly (module.mounts, params.plugins.css) data/homepage.yml: homepage structure, content and sections - including social links, and the hero section.
assets/: Where you can store static assets such as images, CSS, and JavaScript files (you can add custom CSS and JS files with the params.plugins.css in config.toml).
content/: This is where your content files will live. The theme-specific ones are:
content/blog/: For blog posts. content/portfolio/: For portfolio items. content/project/: For projects. content/testimonial/: For testimonials. content/education/: For education items. content/experience/: For experience items. content/client-and-work/: For client and work items. Customizing the theme Hugo allows you to customize the theme in many ways. You can override the theme’s layouts, styles, and content. For that, you just need to locate the file you would like to change, copy it to your site’s corresponding folder (layouts, assets, …), and edit it.
Note: if you do this you will not benefit from theme updates, and that could lead to bugs. You can keep an eye on the UPGRADING.md file.
Improving the theme Maybe some of the customizations you do are worth a share. If you think that your changes could be useful for others, feel free to open a pull request in the GitHub repository - collaborations are very welcome, especially if the contributions come from real-world use cases.
Publishing the site Once you have your site ready, you can publish it to the web. There are many ways to do this, but the recommended one is to use a service like Vercel or Github Pages. Both services offer free hosting for static sites, and they can be connected to your GitHub repository for automatic deployments.
For that, you will need to have a CI/CD action that builds your site and deploys it to the service. You can find an example of a GitHub action in the demo site repository: https://github.com/zetxek/adritian-demo/blob/main/.github/workflows/hugo.yml
title: Create your own version of the site

How to Add Custom Icons to the Adritian Theme Table of Contents Prerequisites Overview Step 1: Export Current Configuration Step 2: Import Configuration to Fontello Step 3: Add New Icons Step 4: Download Updated Font Step 5 (option 1): Update Theme Files Manually Step 5 (option 2): Update Theme Files with npm script Step 6: Using the New Icon Example Usage Troubleshooting Icons Not Displaying Icons Show as Squares Build Errors Best Practices Additional Resources This guide will walk you through adding custom icons to your Adritian Hugo theme. Whether you need new social media icons, brand logos, or custom symbols, follow these steps to integrate them seamlessly.
Prerequisites Before you begin, make sure you have:
Access to your Hugo site’s source files Basic understanding of file management A web browser to access Fontello Overview The Adritian theme uses a custom icon font generated with Fontello. This is a fork of the original fontello, with additional font options.
To add new icons, you’ll need to:
Export the current icon configuration Add new icons using Fontello Download and integrate the updated font files Update your site configuration Step 1: Export Current Configuration Navigate to your theme’s font directory: static/fonts/ Locate the config.json file (see the downstream version) Keep this file ready - you’ll upload it to Fontello Step 2: Import Configuration to Fontello Go to Fontello Click the import button (wrench icon) Upload your config.json file Fontello will load your current icon set Step 3: Add New Icons Browse available icons in Fontello’s library Click on icons you want to add (they’ll be highlighted) Configure icon names by clicking the pencil icon next to each selected icon Set icon codes if needed (Fontello usually assigns these automatically) Step 4: Download Updated Font Click the Download webfont button in Fontello Save the generated ZIP file to your computer Extract the ZIP file contents Step 5 (option 1): Update Theme Files Manually Copy font files from the downloaded ZIP to static/fonts/:
Copy .woff, .woff2, .ttf, and .eot files Update CSS file:
Open the CSS file from the ZIP Important: Replace all instances of /font with /fonts Copy the updated CSS to your theme’s CSS file Replace config.json:
Copy the new config.json from the ZIP to static/fonts/ Step 5 (option 2): Update Theme Files with npm script You can use the theme helper (https://www.npmjs.com/package/@zetxek/adritian-theme-helper) to update the theme files.
You can read the theme helper font script here: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@zetxek/adritian-theme-helper#user-content-update-font-script
With the following command you can update the theme files with the new icons automatically:
ts-node scripts/update-font.ts <source> <destination> Step 6: Using the New Icon Reference your new icons in your content, as for the pre-provided icons.
Example Usage <!-- In your templates --> <i class="icon-your-new-icon-name"></i> <!-- In markdown with HTML --> <i class="icon-your-new-icon-name"></i> Custom Icon Text <!-- In a markdown file --> { {< link icon="icon-your-new-icon-name" url="https://example.com" >} } Note: for the markdown file, no spaces between the curly braces - added so it gets displayed here properly.
Troubleshooting Icons Not Displaying Check file paths: Ensure fonts are in static/fonts/ Verify CSS paths: Make sure /font is changed to /fonts Clear browser cache: Force refresh with Ctrl+F5 (or Cmd+Shift+R on Mac) Icons Show as Squares Font files missing: Verify all font files were copied correctly CSS not loaded: Check that your CSS includes the new icon definitions Build Errors Invalid CSS: Check for syntax errors in your CSS file Missing files: Ensure all required font files are present Best Practices Keep backups: Save your old config.json before making changes Test locally: Always test icon changes on your local development site first Consistent naming: Use clear, descriptive names for your custom icons Optimize selection: Only include icons you actually need to keep font file sizes small Do not modify the theme, override the files in your own project: Instead of modifying the theme, override the files in your own site project. That will ensure you can update the theme without losing your changes. If your icon choice is a popular one, consider contributing it to the theme: If you think your icon choice is a popular one, consider contributing it to the theme. That will help other users and make the theme more complete. Additional Resources Fontello Documentation Adritian Theme Icons - View all available icons Need help? If you encounter issues following this guide, check the theme’s GitHub repository for support and examples. If you still need help, you can open a new issue in the theme’s GitHub repository.
title: How to Add Custom Icons to the Adritian Theme

Paper source: BLIP: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training (arXiv) My full notes on GitHub: paper-reviews/BLIP
Introduction Limitations of Previous Studies No single model architecture performed well on both text generation and image-text retrieval tasks. Text generation: given a cat image, generate text such as “A photo of a black cat lying on the floor.” Image-text retrieval: given the image and the text, verify whether the image–text pair matches. Past architectures had complementary weaknesses: Encoder-based models lack a decoder, so they struggle with text generation. Encoder-decoder models lack a mechanism to force matching images and texts to align, so their retrieval performance is low — the loss only checks whether the output is reasonable, not whether two vectors lie in the same embedding space. Using raw web text is suboptimal for vision-language learning, because web text contains noise that hurts the model. Characteristics of BLIP Multimodal mixture of Encoder-Decoder (MED) Mixes an encoder-based and an encoder-decoder–based model in one architecture. Handles multiple tasks from a single architecture, reorganizing its modules per task for flexibility. Captioning and Filtering (CapFilt) After pre-training the MED, fine-tuning produces a captioner and a filter that improve the noisy web-text dataset. Captioner: generates synthetic captions from web images. Filter: given the synthetic caption and the web text, removes the noisy one. Related Work Vision-Language Pre-training Pre-trains a single model on large amounts of paired image–text data, learning the joint representation of both modalities. The model is not task-specific, so further fine-tuning is required for downstream tasks. Prior work largely ignored the impact of noise; this paper aims to address it and to unify generation-based and understanding-based tasks. Knowledge Distillation (KD) A student (small) model mimics the behavior of a teacher (large) model by matching the distribution the teacher outputs. BLIP applies KD in spirit: captioner and filter work together to provide a better training dataset for MED. Data Augmentation (DA) DA for NLP has been less active than for computer vision. The team uses the captioner to generate synthetic captions as augmentation. Model Architecture Architecture: MED Consists of three parts: Unimodal encoder Separately encodes image (ViT) and text (BERT-style encoder with bidirectional self-attention). A [CLS] token is prepended to the text to summarize the sentence. Image-grounded text encoder Encodes text with an [Encode] token (bidirectional self-attention), then incorporates image information through cross-attention. The [Encode] token embedding serves as the multimodal representation of the image–text pair. Image-grounded text decoder Uses masked self-attention to predict future tokens and cross-attention for image information. Training: input starts with [Decode] and ends with [EOS]; using teacher forcing, the decoder generates tokens, with cross-entropy loss at each position. Inference: given [Decode], the decoder outputs token by token from previous words. Losses Image-Text Contrastive Loss (ITC) — enforces positive image–text pairs to align versus negatives. A momentum encoder accumulates historical weights, and the main encoder matches the soft labels (probability distribution over candidates) it outputs. Soft labels handle false negatives common in web data. Image-Text Matching Loss (ITM) — a finer-grained binary classification (0/1 from the [Encode] token) using hard negative mining: negatives more similar to the positive are more likely sampled, enabling fine-grained alignment. Language Modeling Loss (LM) — assigns high probability to true tokens given image and previous tokens; cross-entropy per position with label smoothing of 0.1. Parameter sharing: the text encoder and decoder share all parameters except the self-attention layers (bidirectional vs. masked). Architecture: CapFilt Problem with raw web texts: alt-texts paired with images are often noisy (e.g. “Click for more…”). Solution — CapFilt: Captioner is created by fine-tuning the LM objective; it generates synthetic captions for a web image. Filter is created by fine-tuning the ITC & ITM objectives; it removes false captions by comparing web image–synthetic caption and web image–web text pairs. Filtered pairs are concatenated with human-annotated pairs to form a new dataset, and MED is pre-trained again on it. Experiments Case Studies Effect of captioner and filter — combinations of {no C/F, no C, no F, both} were tried; the model using both filter and captioner performed best. Diversity of captions — comparing beam search (most likely full sequence) and nucleus sampling (smallest token set whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold); nucleus sampling performed best despite producing noisier captions. Parameter sharing — sharing all layers except self-attention performed best, with the bonus of reducing model size. Task Studies Image-text retrieval — fine-tuned on COCO, tested on Flickr30K; BLIP outperformed existing models. Image captioning — on COCO and NoCaps, BLIP outperformed others using a similar amount of pre-training data; BLIP with 129M images matched LEMON (which uses 200M images and heavier computation). Visual Question Answering (VQA) — the image-grounded text encoder processes image–question pairs, and the decoder generates an answer. Natural Language Visual Reasoning (NLVR²) — multiple image encoders and image-grounded text encoders, with a merge layer before the 0/1 decision. Visual Dialog (VisDial) — VQA extended to conversation; separate image and caption encoders feed a dialog encoder with the dialog history and question.
title: BLIP: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training for Unified Vision-Language Understanding and Generation

As a participant in the QI AI Research Program, I first completed a hands-on training track using KNIME, a no-code machine learning platform, to build foundations in end-to-end ML workflows — data preprocessing, feature engineering, model training, and evaluation.
I then led a team research project as first author of the paper “Development of Machine Learning Models for Spatio-Temporal Pattern Analysis of High-Volume For-Hire Vehicle Demand in Manhattan” — accepted to the Korea Computer Congress (KCC), hosted by the Korean Institute of Information Scientists and Engineers (KIISE). The study proposes a grid-based hourly demand forecasting framework for ride-hailing services (Uber, Lyft) using Random Forest Regression trained on NYC TLC trip records and Open-Meteo weather data. By re-partitioning Manhattan into a uniform 14×8 grid (34 valid cells), we addressed the spatial inconsistency of conventional taxi zones and modeled non-linear spatio-temporal demand patterns with cyclic time encodings and 24-hour lag features.
Key findings: weather variables degraded predictive performance during the study window (acting as noise), while the demand-only model achieved an average SMAPE of 13.1% and RMSE of 35.85 across grids — robust performance with reduced computational cost. We further diagnosed elevated error in two low-demand, high-volatility grid cells and proposed deep learning extensions for future work.

My full notes on GitHub: paper-reviews/Automated Sewing System
Introduction Previous Technologies Earlier computer-vision tools could recognize shapes, generate sewing paths, and govern parts of the assembly But they Struggled to generate stitching paths for overlapped patches using edge-detection algorithms Required human intervention — the stitching wasn’t fully automated Goal Build a pattern former that Produces a seam-line detection algorithm Generates paths for top stitches Components of the Pattern Former Sewing Unit — performs automatic sewing X-y Stage — moves the fabric horizontally and vertically Template — holds the fabric, exposing the overlapped target layers Pipeline Step 1 — Infer the Template Window with Instance Segmentation What is instance segmentation? Provides pixel-level boundaries (e.g. “this pixel is inside the template window, that one isn’t”) Tool: fine-tuned YOLOv5 Backbone — extracts features via convolution and downsampling Neck — upsamples small feature maps and merges them with larger ones, outputting multi-scale features Head — predicts bounding boxes, masks, and classes for each scale; merges into a final prediction Fine-tuning details Problem 1: images are too large to convolve — resize them Problem 2: uneven lighting (center brighter than edges) — apply CLAHE to redistribute brightness, then Gaussian Blur to smooth Problem 3: the template window is small, so detail in the seam-line region is lost — augment by splitting each image into 16 tiles and upsampling Inference The full sewing setup is captured Only CLAHE + Gaussian Blur are applied (no resizing or tiling) The template window is localized Step 2 — Seam-Line Detection Seam lines are detected by how light reflects off different fabric regions Lighting is positioned asymmetrically to the camera to amplify reflectance differences — the seam line reflects minimal light Algorithm For each column, find local minima — gather five candidate seam-line points Select the seam line by minimizing the index difference between candidates across columns Smooth the detected points to form the seam line Step 3 — Generate the Top-Stitch Path Offset a fixed distance from the seam line to produce the top-stitch path Step 4 — Sewing Machine Performs Top Stitching The system comprises a sewing machine, a camera, and lighting ROS (Robot Operating System) handles inter-node communication via topics — channels that nodes publish to and subscribe from Node breakdown Sewing-machine node — controls the x-y stage and reads motor-encoder positions Vision node — captures fabric images and runs the detection algorithm Light node — manages LED light sources GUI node — lets the operator monitor and control stitching Limitations Does not work for all fabrics Matte/dark patterns make light-reflection differences hard to detect Large mesh patterns with holes create multiple local minima, requiring extra image processing
title: Automated Sewing System Enabled by Machine Vision for Smart Garment Manufacturing

My full notes on GitHub: paper-reviews/STSGCN
Introduction Previous Technologies Earlier traffic forecasting models Capture relationships across either time or space (rarely both at once) Learn the spatial relationship first, then feed it into a temporal model Limitations In reality, time and space information move together, but earlier models treat them sequentially Data patterns vary across times and regions, but earlier architectures reuse the same module for all locations/periods Goal of STSGCN Build a spatio-temporal forecasting framework that can Detect complex localized spatial-temporal correlations with a synchronous modeling mechanism Use multiple modules across different time spans to identify heterogeneities in localized spatial-temporal graphs Architecture Input Spatial-temporal network series $X_\mathcal{G} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C \times T}$ — raw node data from spatial graphs in continuous time periods Each spatial graph at time $t$ has a signal matrix $X_\mathcal{G}^{(t)}$ and adjacency matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}$ Input Transformation Fully-connected layer projects features for better representation: $$\mathbf{H^{(0)} = \sigma(X_\mathcal{G} W_{in} + b_{in})} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C’ \times T}$$ Spatial-temporal embedding adds learned spatial ($S_{emb}$) and temporal ($T_{emb}$) embeddings, broadcast across the other dimension: $$\tilde{H}^{(0)} = H^{(0)} + T_{emb} + S_{emb}$$ Spatial-Temporal Synchronous Graph Convolutional Layer (STSGCL) STSGCM (the building block) Input: a localized spatial-temporal graph signal matrix $h^{(0)} \in \mathbb{R}^{3N \times C}$ — connects each node at time $t$ with itself at $t-1$ and $t+1$ Adjacency matrix $A’ \in \mathbb{R}^{3N \times 3N}$ Graph convolution: $$GCN(h^{(l-1)}) = h^{(l)} = \sigma(A’ h^{(l-1)} W + b) \in \mathbb{R}^{3N \times C’}$$ Activation: GLU works best; multiple convolutional layers are stacked Aggregation: max-pool across stacked layers to filter useless features Cropping: keep only the current time-step nodes (neighbouring time information is already absorbed via convolution) Final output: $h^{(final)} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C}$ STSGCM captures localized spatial-temporal correlation — how one node influences other nodes’ future states.
From STSGCM to STSGCL Within one layer, multiple STSGCMs with different weights handle heterogeneity across the long time span Layer input: $X \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times N \times C}$; each STSGCM operates on a cropped $X’ \in \mathbb{R}^{3N \times C}$ Layer output: $M = [M_1, M_2, \ldots, M_{T-2}] \in \mathbb{R}^{(T-2) \times N \times C_{out}}$ Stacking layers Extends the temporal span the model can integrate (correlation) Enables deeper, more abstract features (heterogeneity) Output Two FC layers convert the final STSGCL output into a 12-step prediction: $$\hat{Y}=[\hat{y}^{(1)},…,\hat{y}^{(12)}] \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times T’}$$ Extra Components Mask matrix — adjacency is binary, but neighbors influence the center node to different degrees. Use a learnable mask $W_{mask}$: $$A’{adjusted} = W{mask} \otimes A’ \in \mathbb{R}^{3N \times 3N}$$ Huber loss — less sensitive to outliers than squared error: $$L(Y, \hat{Y}) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}(Y - \hat{Y})^2 & |Y - \hat{Y}| \leq \delta \ \delta|Y - \hat{Y}| - \frac{1}{2}\delta^2 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ Experiments Settings Datasets: PEMS03, PEMS04, PEMS07, PEMS08 (4 districts), aggregated in 5-minute intervals Use the previous hour of traffic to predict the next hour Graph: nodes are sensors; edges connect sensors on the same road Values standardized Splits & Training 6 : 2 : 2 train/val/test ratio All experiments repeated 10 times Best architecture: 4 STSGCL layers, each with 3 graph convolutional operations (64, 64, 64 filters) Baselines Graph WaveNet, STG2Seq, and other established traffic-forecasting baselines
title: Spatial-Temporal Synchronous Graph Convolutional Networks (STSGCN)

Paper source: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (arXiv) My full notes on GitHub: paper-reviews/CLIP
Introduction Goal Propose Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training (CLIP) — an architecture that performs zero-shot transfer for image classification on datasets that weren’t used in pre-training Motivation NLP had huge success pre-training models on raw web text rather than crowd-labeled datasets Could the same paradigm shift happen in computer vision? Architecture Components Natural Language Supervision Use phrases written by real people instead of artificial labels Advantages Easier to gather than crowd-labeled data (no fixed format) Connects image and language information Dataset 400 million English text–image pairs scraped and filtered from the Internet Pre-Training Method A generative objective (predicting exact captions) was too expensive The team settled on a contrastive objective: train an image encoder and a text encoder so that paired images and texts have high cosine similarity in a shared embedding space Optimized with symmetric cross-entropy loss The dataset was so large that overfitting was not a concern Model Selection and Scaling Image encoder: ResNet-50 and Vision Transformer (ViT) — patch images, linearly project, add positional and [CLS] embeddings, feed through a Transformer encoder Text encoder: Transformer Scaling: increased both width (channels) and depth (layers) simultaneously Model Architecture Inference Phase Encode all candidate label texts and the input image Project into the shared embedding space Dot-product similarities → softmax → class probabilities Experiments Zero-Shot Transfer Used prompt engineering and ensembling to handle polysemy Template: “a photo of {label}, a type of {category}” Average over multiple worded variants (small/big/etc.) Performance Baseline 1: ResNet-50 features + fully supervised logistic regression Zero-shot CLIP wins on 16 of 27 datasets Underperforms on specialized/abstract tasks (satellite imagery, tumor detection) Baseline 2: Few-shot methods (frozen CLIP encoder + logistic regression on features) Zero-shot CLIP ≈ 4-shot logistic regression Upper bound: Fully supervised classifiers CLIP zero-shot is 10–25% below; closer on datasets where linear probing achieves >90% — hinting CLIP excels when data is high quality Representation Learning Measured via linear probing on frozen features (rather than fine-tuning, which masks encoder quality) Large CLIP ResNets slightly outperform EfficientNet-NoisyStudent CLIP ViTs are ~3× more compute-efficient than CLIP ResNets Robustness to Natural Distribution Shift Natural distribution shifts arise from real-world changes in environment/camera/people; synthetic shifts come from manual modifications Two metrics: effective robustness (improvement above the expected in-distribution↔OOD line) and relative robustness (raw OOD gain) All zero-shot CLIP models show effective robustness Adapting CLIP to ImageNet improves on ImageNet but lowers average performance — caution when using ImageNet as the robustness benchmark Robustness intervention Class label misalignment between train and test taxonomies — traditional classifiers struggle, but CLIP’s shared embedding space generalizes (e.g. correctly maps “baseball player” to “person”) Human Comparison On Oxford-IIIT Pet breeds, humans jump from 54% (zero-shot) → 76% with one example per class CLIP doesn’t show this jump from 1-shot, suggesting humans leverage prior knowledge differently Data Overlap Analysis Run a duplicate detector over each evaluation dataset → split into Overlap / Clean / All Measure contamination as Overlap/All; compare accuracy on Overlap vs Clean Median overlap is 2.2%, average 3.2% — accuracy change rarely exceeds 0.1% Concerns: detector imperfect (CIFAR-100 false positives); class-distribution shifts may also drive accuracy differences Limitations Low computational and data efficiency Below task-specific models on fine-grained classification (cars, flowers, aircraft) Weak on abstract/systematic tasks (counting objects) Random-level performance on novel out-of-distribution tasks (e.g. distance to nearest car); even loses to logistic regression on raw MNIST pixels Limited to a fixed candidate label set — generative approaches can produce free-form labels but cost more compute Still data-inefficient Evaluation datasets may share distribution with training data Training data is unfiltered and may carry social biases Some visual concepts are hard to express in text CLIP doesn’t learn like humans — hybrid zero/few-shot remains open Broader Impacts Bias Class taxonomy choices can encode social inequalities; adding non-human and crime labels to the classifier exposes uneven distributions across race/gender/age subgroups Surveillance Coarse classification: ~91.8% on CCTV imagery, dropping to 51.1% in a stress test Fine-grained classification: chance-level Celebrity recognition from CCTV is worse than Google’s Celebrity Recognition Conclusion CLIP is a zero-shot learner that generalizes across many tasks unseen during pre-training Still trails domain-specific supervised models, with room to grow
title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (CLIP)

Paper source: SMPL: A Skinned Multi-Person Linear Model (ResearchGate) My full notes on GitHub: paper-reviews/SMPL
Introduction Goal Creating an animation that can represent human body with different shapes and natural poses It must also be compatible to the current technology SMPL Model in Brief Learn blend shapes to correct unrealistic deformations Blending process uses a linear function of the elements of each part’s rotation matrix This makes the model simple enough for training and animating How SMPL is Built Learning pose-related parameters Data: 1786 scans of different people in different poses Process Align the template mesh to each scan Then, optimize the following by minimizing the vertex error: blend weights, pose-dependent blend shapes, the rest pose, and a regressor Learning identity-related parameters Data: CAESAR dataset (~2000 scans per gender) Process Align the template mesh to each scan Pose-normalize the data (so that only the shape variation remains) Run a PCA on the resulting vertices to get outputs Evaluation Qualitative Standard: Compare with side-by-side animations Quantitative Standard: Compare the vertex errors with the test data Static Model Comparison E.g. Comparing people with still poses In the paper, BlendSCAPE is used as a baseline model to compare with SMPL BlendSCAPE is triangle deformation-based while SMPL is vertex-based Dynamic Model Comparison E.g. Comparing soft-tissue dynamics like belly bouncing In the paper, Dyna is used as a baseline model to compare with Dynamic-SMPL (DMPL) Dyna is triangle deformation-based while DMPL is vertex-based Related Work Blend Skinning Definition: Attaching the surface of a mesh to an underlying skeletal structure Each vertex in the mesh surface is relocated by the weighted influence of their neighboring bones Limitations Produce unrealistic deformations at joints Auto-rigging Definition: Process of automatically building a skeleton inside a 3D mesh Limitations They don’t learn corrective blend shapes They may not generalize well to new poses and motions They do not span a space of body shapes Blend Shapes Definition: Corrective offsets that will be added to the rest pose before applying a skinning equation (LBS) Limitations Corrective offsets should be calculated for each pose Others Most methods focus on learning a single-shape model → The paper aims to propose a model that can represent diverse human poses Some of them use triangle deformation that has expressive power, but they are not compatible with the existing software → The paper aims to solve this with a vertex-based model that still has an expressive power Model Formulation Goal $$M(\vec{\beta},\vec{\theta};\Phi):\mathbb{R}^{|\vec{\theta}| \times |\vec{\beta}|} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{3N}$$
The model receives inputs of shape and pose parameters ($\vec{\beta}$ and $\vec{\theta}$), and learned model parameters $\Phi$. Then it aims to output $(x, y, z)$ coordinates of $N$ points that comprise the 3D body mesh, in the transformed location.
Blend Skinning $$\bar{t}i’ = \sum{k=1}^{K} w_{k,i} , G_k’\bigl(\vec{\theta}, J(\vec{\beta})\bigr) \left( \bar{t}i + b{S,i}(\vec{\beta}) + b_{P,i}(\vec{\theta}) \right)$$
The displacement $\bar{t}i’$ is the weighted sum of joint contributions — weights $w{k,i}$, joint-driven rotation $G_k’$, and the rest-pose vertex plus shape/pose blend shape offsets.
Shape Blend Shapes $\vec{\beta}$ is a collection of linear shape coefficients (e.g., height, weight tendency). $S$ is a learned parameter of shape displacements. Their dot product gives an identity-dependent offset for all vertices.
$$B_S(\vec{\beta}; S) = \sum_{n=1}^{|\vec{\beta}|} \beta_n S_n$$
Pose Blend Shapes $$B_P(\vec{\theta}; P) = \sum_{n=1}^{9K} \left( R_n(\vec{\theta}) - R_n(\vec{\theta}^*) \right) P_n$$
Each term scales a learned mesh deformation $P_n$ by how much a single rotation-matrix entry deviates from the rest pose.
Joint Locations $$J(\vec{\beta}; \mathcal{J}, \bar{T}, S) = \mathcal{J}\left(\bar{T} + B_S(\vec{\beta}; S)\right)$$
$\mathcal{J}$ is a learned mapping that regresses joint positions from vertex coordinates.
Recap Step 1: Apply shape and pose blend shapes to the rest template. Step 2: For each joint, compute its weighted rotational influence on each vertex. Step 3: Apply the rotations to the displaced vertices; sum for the final location. Training Datasets Multi-pose: 1789 registrations of 40 individuals Multi-shape: 1700 (male) + 2100 (female) registrations Plan Train $\Phi = { \bar{\mathbf{T}}, \mathcal{W, S, J, P} }$ to minimize vertex reconstruction error Train ${\mathcal{J, W, P}}$ on the multi-pose dataset, then ${\bar{\mathbf{T}}, \mathcal{S}}$ on the multi-shape dataset Men and women have separate parameters Pose Parameter Training (alternating optimization) Optimize $\vec{\theta}_j$ holding others fixed Optimize ${\hat{\mathbf{T}}_i^P, \hat{\mathbf{J}}_i^P}$ Optimize ${\mathcal{W}, \mathcal{P}}$ Repeat until convergence Optimize $\mathcal{J}$ last Shape Parameter Training Estimate pose, then pose-normalize each figure Solve for rest-pose shape $\hat{\mathbf{T}}_j^S$ Run PCA over ${\hat{\mathbf{T}}_j^S}$ to get ${\bar{\mathbf{T}}, \mathcal{S}}$ Evaluation Model generalization: fit to new people and new poses Pose generalization: generalize a person’s shape to new poses Sparse SMPL (limiting joint influence per vertex) did not improve performance Run-time: SMPL is faster than its SCAPE baseline Compatibility: built on standard skinning, so it works in existing 3D animation software DMPL: Dynamic SMPL Adds dynamic blend shapes to model soft-tissue dynamics (e.g. bouncing belly) Driven by a dynamic control vector $\vec{\phi}_t = [\dot{\vec{\theta}}_t, \ddot{\vec{\theta}}_t, \mathbf{v}t, \mathbf{a}t, \vec{\delta}{t-1}, \vec{\delta}{t-2}]$ $\mathcal{D}$ learned via PCA; prediction: $B_D(\vec{\phi}_t, \vec{\beta}; \mathcal{D}) = \mu_D + \mathcal{D}f(\vec{\phi}_t, \vec{\beta})$ Discussion Linearity is the key advantage — enables training on large data Limitations: hard to model non-realistic characters; does not capture joint-independent motion (breathing, facial motion, muscle tension)
title: SMPL: A Skinned Multi-Person Linear Model

Shortcodes are a convenient functionality of Hugo, allowing you to embed templates or layouts within other content.
Some of the example built-in shortcodes are Instagram posts, YouTube videos, QR codes, etc. You can find the full list in the official docs.
The theme provides custom shortcodes to allow you to customize your landing page as you want:
toc: Generates a styled table of contents from page headings. education-list: Displays a list of educational qualifications. experience-list: Shows a list of professional experiences. platform-links: Embeds links to various platforms with icons. newsletter-section: Adds a section for newsletter subscription. - link: Creates a hyperlink with an icon. experience-section: Inserts a detailed experience section. contact-section: Adds a contact information section, with a customizable form and information. client-and-work-section: Displays a section for clients and work. about-section: About section, with image, buttons for call to action and image. testimonial-section: Adds references from customers, colleagues, etc. showcase: two-column block with a full-width image to the left, and a text snippet to the right. Great for a call to action or introduction of the person (assuming it’s a personal website). text-section: utility shortcode used to render text in some parts of the theme where it would otherwise be full-width, appearing “too floaty”. See the github issue #260 for context. spacer: Adds vertical spacing before the next element. The shortcodes can be customized with different arguments:
toc: Automatically generates a table of contents from the page’s headings (H2, H3, etc.)
heading: Custom heading text for the table of contents. Defaults to “Table of Contents”. showHeading: Boolean value to show or hide the heading. Defaults to true. class: Custom CSS class for styling. Defaults to “table-of-contents”. Features: Only displays if the page contains headings Supports nested heading levels with proper indentation Responsive design with dark mode support Smooth scrolling to sections Clean, modern styling with hover effects Usage Examples: {{< toc >}}: Basic table of contents with default settings {{< toc heading="Contents" >}}: Custom heading {{< toc showHeading=false >}}: Hide the heading {{< toc class="sidebar-toc" >}}: Custom CSS class {{< toc heading="Article Contents" class="custom-toc" >}}: Multiple parameters education-list:
title: The title of the education section. items: A list of educational qualifications, they’re provided by the education content type pages. From each, the year, university, and degree will be used. sectionId: Optional. Overrides the default HTML id for the section. If not provided, the default id is used. experience-list:
title: The title of the experience section (optional). When provided, an h2 heading is added above the list. padding: Controls whether the section has padding. Set to “true” by default. items: A list of professional experiences, coming from the experience content type. For each of them, the companyLogo, duration, jobTitle, location, and Content are used. Note: On mobile devices, a separator line is automatically added between experience entries for better readability. sectionId: Optional. Overrides the default HTML id for the section. If not provided, the default id is used. platform-links:
platforms: A container to place social links inside. Usually you’ll want to use it with a list of link nested (see below) sectionId: Optional. Overrides the default HTML id for the section. If not provided, the default id is used. link: links to social platforms (facebook, linkedin, etc)
url: The URL for the hyperlink. icon: The icon to display with the link. sectionId: Optional. Overrides the default HTML id for the section. If not provided, the default id is used. newsletter-section:
Form Configuration: form_action: The URL where the newsletter form data will be submitted. Falls back to site data configuration (typically set in data/homepage.yaml). form_method: The HTTP method for form submission (typically “POST” or “GET”). Falls back to site data configuration. Section Content: newsletter_title: Sets the main heading/title for the newsletter section. Falls back to i18n value “newsletter_title”. newsletter_placeholder: Placeholder text displayed in the email input field. Falls back to i18n value “newsletter_placeholder”. newsletter_button: Text displayed on the subscription button. Falls back to i18n value “newsletter_button”. Response Messages: newsletter_success_message: Message displayed to users after successful subscription. Falls back to i18n value “newsletter_success_message”. newsletter_error_message: Message displayed to users if subscription fails. Falls back to i18n value “newsletter_error_message”. newsletter_note: Small text/disclaimer shown below the form (typically mentions privacy policy). Falls back to i18n value “newsletter_note”. sectionId: Optional. Overrides the default HTML id for the section. If not provided, the default id is used. experience-section:
title: The title of the experience section. experiences: A detailed list of experiences, coming from the experience content type pages. sectionId: Optional. Overrides the default HTML id for the section. If not provided, the default id is used. contact-section:
title: Sets the main heading/title for the contact section. Falls back to the i18n value “contact_title” if not provided. Form Configuration: form_action: The URL where the form data will be submitted. Commonly used with services like Formspree. Falls back to site data configuration. form_method: The HTTP method for form submission (typically “POST” or “GET”). Falls back to site data configuration. Form Field Placeholders: contact_form_name: Placeholder text for the name input field. Falls back to i18n value. contact_form_email: Placeholder text for the email input field. Falls back to i18n value. contact_form_phone: Placeholder text for the phone input field. Falls back to i18n value. contact_form_message: Placeholder text for the message textarea. Falls back to i18n value. contact_form_rows: Number of rows for the message textarea. Defaults to 2 if not specified. contact_button: Text for the form submission button. Falls back to i18n value. Contact Information: contact_phone_title: Heading for the phone contact section. Falls back to i18n value. contact_phone_number: Phone number to display. Falls back to i18n value. contact_email_title: Heading for the email contact section. Falls back to i18n value. contact_email_email: Email address to display. Falls back to i18n value. contact_address_title: Heading for the address section. Falls back to i18n value. contact_address_address: Physical address or location information. Falls back to i18n value. sectionId: Optional. Overrides the default HTML id for the section. If not provided, the default id is used. client-and-work-section: this shortcode doesn’t use as many arguments - as much of the content comes from other content pages.
title: The title of the client and work section. clients: A list of clients, coming from the client content type (each with title, link, logo) projects: A list of projects, coming from the project content type (each with title, content, button.URL, button.btnText, button.icon, image). sectionId: Optional. Overrides the default HTML id for the section. If not provided, the default id is used. about-section:
Content Arguments
intro_title - Sets the main heading/title for the about section. Falls back to the title from site data if not provided.
intro_description - Contains the HTML content or description text for the about section. Falls back to the content from site data if not provided.
imgSrc - Specifies the path to the image displayed in the about section. Falls back to the image defined in site data if not provided.
imgWidth - Specifies the width for the image.
imgHeight - Specifies the height for the image.
imgScale - Specifies the scale used for the image (for example, 0.5 if the high resolution image is double the size of the smaller one) This is only considered if neither imgWidth nor imgHeight is used.
text_align - Controls the vertical alignment of the text content relative to the image. Accepts “center” (default), “top”, or “bottom”.
Primary Button Arguments
button1_enable - Boolean value to show or hide the primary button. Defaults to the value from site data.
button1_icon - icon class to display before the button text. Falls back to the icon from site data.
button1_url - Target URL for the primary button. Falls back to the URL from site data.
button1_text - Text label to display on the primary button. Falls back to the text from site data.
Secondary Button Arguments
button2_enable - Boolean value to show or hide the secondary button. Defaults to the value from site data.
button2_icon - FontAwesome or icon class to display before the button text. Falls back to the icon from site data.
button2_url - Target URL for the secondary button. Falls back to the URL from site data.
button2_text - Text label to display on the secondary button. Falls back to the text from site data.
sectionId: Optional. Overrides the default HTML id for the section. If not provided, the default id is used.
testimonial-section:
title: The title of the testimonial section. testimonials: A list of testimonials, provided by the testimonial content type pages. The partial dynamically pulls content from pages with type “testimonial”. Each testimonial page should include: Content: The main testimonial text (the actual quote) Meta Information: name: The name of the person giving the testimonial position: The job title or role of the person giving the testimonial image.src: Path to the image of the testimonial author sectionId: Optional. Overrides the default HTML id for the section. If not provided, the default id is used. showcase:
Content Arguments: title: Sets the main heading/title for the showcase section. Falls back to the i18n value “showcase_title”. subtitle: Sets the subtitle text that appears below the main heading. Falls back to the i18n value “showcase_subtitle”. description: Contains the HTML content or description text for the showcase section. Falls back to the i18n value “showcase_description”. Button Configuration: button_text: Text label to display on the button. If not provided or set to false, the button will not be displayed. button_icon: Icon class to display before the button text. Falls back to the icon from site data. button_url: Target URL for the button. Falls back to the URL from site data. Image Configuration: imgSrc: Specifies the path to the image displayed in the showcase section. Falls back to the image defined in site data. imgWidth - Specifies the width for the image. imgHeight - Specifies the height for the image. imgScale - Specifies the scale used for the image (for example, 0.5 if the high resolution image is double the size of the smaller one) This is only considered if neither imgWidth nor imgHeight is used. Social Media: social_links: Array of social media platform links to display at the bottom of the showcase. Each item should have a URL and icon property. Responsive Behavior: The showcase uses a two-column layout on desktop devices (≥768px) and stacks columns vertically on mobile devices, with the image appearing above the text content. Inner Content: The shortcode can also accept inner content that will be rendered in a separate div with class “inner-content”. sectionId: Optional. Overrides the default HTML id for the section. If not provided, the default id is used. text-section:
Content Arguments: title: Sets the main heading/title for the text section (optional). subtitle: Sets the subtitle text that appears below the main heading (optional). Layout Options: padding: Controls whether the section has padding. Set to “true” by default. centered: When set to “true”, adds flexbox classes to center the content both horizontally and vertically. Set to “false” by default. Inner Content: The shortcode accepts markdown-formatted inner content that will be rendered in the text section. sectionId: Optional. Overrides the default HTML id for the section. If not provided, the default id is used. spacer:
Size Options: size: Controls the amount of vertical spacing. Accepts “small”, “medium” (default), “large”, or “xlarge”. Usage Examples: {{< spacer >}}: Adds medium spacing (default) {{< spacer size="small" >}}: Adds minimal spacing {{< spacer size="large" >}}: Adds substantial spacing {{< spacer size="xlarge" >}}: Adds maximum spacing sectionId: Optional. Overrides the default HTML id for the section. If not provided, the default id is used. You can see them in effect in:
